item.title: 1947: Sam Breadon and His Minority Partners Sell the St. Louis Cardinals
item.description: Sam Breadon and his minority partners sell the St. Louis Cardinals to former United States Postmaster General Robert E. Hannegan, 44, and St. Louis attorney Fred Saigh, 42. Breadon, 71, became the Redbirds' president and largest stockholder in 1920 and principal owner two years later; under him they won nine National League pennants and six World Series titles. Photo: St. Louis Cardinals - 1941 Team Issue (Public domain).

item.title: 2015: Gallego Was Announced as Director of Baseball Development for the Los
item.description: On November 25, 2015, Gallego was announced as director of baseball development for the Los Angeles Angels of Anaheim. Photo: Scott U (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2011: Davis Was Hired to Be the Oakland Athletics Hitting Coach
item.description: On November 25, 2011, Davis was hired to be the Oakland Athletics hitting coach. Photo: Barry Colla (Public domain).

item.title: 2011: Yukio Nishimoto, 91, Japanese Baseball Hall of Fame Player and Manager
item.description: Yukio Nishimoto, 91, Japanese Baseball Hall of Fame player and manager. Photo: ベースボール・マガジン社（Baseball Magazine Co. Ltd) (Public domain).

item.title: 2010: Free Agent Kaz Matsui Returns to Japan, Signing
item.description: Free agent Kaz Matsui returns to Japan, signing with the Rakuten Eagles of the Japanese Pacific League. Photo: えすぱにぃ (CC BY-SA 4.0).

item.title: 2006: Krynzel Was Drafted in the 1st Round (11th Overall) of the 2000 Major
item.description: Krynzel was drafted in the 1st round (11th overall) of the 2000 Major League Baseball draft and spent seven years in the Milwaukee Brewers farm system before being traded to the Arizona Diamondbacks on November 25, 2006, with Doug Davis and Dana Eveland for Johnny Estrada, Greg Aquino, and Claudio Vargas. Photo: Jeramey Jannene: Flickr, website (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 2005: The Baltimore Orioles Signed Tatís to a Minor-League Contract
item.description: The Baltimore Orioles signed Tatís to a minor-league contract on November 25, 2005. Photo: Wknight94 (CC BY-SA 3.0).

item.title: 2002: The Boston Red Sox Sign 28-Year–old Theo Epstein
item.description: The Boston Red Sox sign 28-year–old Theo Epstein as their new general manager. He becomes the youngest GM in major league history. Photo: Scott Slingsby from Rochester, NH (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 1993: Burgess Whitehead, 83, Last Surviving Member of the St. Louis
item.description: Burgess Whitehead, 83, last surviving member of the St. Louis Cardinals Gashouse Gang team that won 95 games, the National League pennant, and the 1934 World Series in seven games over the Detroit Tigers.

item.title: 1991: The Montreal Expos Trade First Baseman Andrés Galarraga to the St
item.description: The Montreal Expos trade first baseman Andrés Galarraga to the St. Louis Cardinals for starting pitcher Ken Hill. Galarraga struggles for St. Louis before enjoying a career renaissance with the Colorado Rockies in 1993. Photo: User Dlz28 on en.wikipedia (Public domain).

item.title: 1986: Jose Canseco of the Oakland Athletics, Who Hit .240
item.description: Jose Canseco of the Oakland Athletics, who hit .240 with 33 home runs and 117 RBI, wins the American League Rookie of the Year Award with 16 of 28 first place votes, with the others going to Wally Joyner of the California Angels (.290, 22, 100). Canseco also becomes the first Athletics franchise player to win the award since pitcher Harry Byrd in 1952. Photo: Glenn Francis (CC BY-SA 4.0).

item.title: 1985: The Rangers Traded Schmidt Along
item.description: The Rangers traded Schmidt along with Wayne Tolleson to the White Sox for Scott Fletcher, Edwin Correa, and José Mota on November 25, 1985. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1981: Rollie Fingers of the Milwaukee Brewers Becomes the First Relief
item.description: Rollie Fingers of the Milwaukee Brewers becomes the first relief pitcher ever to win the American League Most Valuable Player Award, edging out Rickey Henderson of the Oakland Athletics, 319 to 308. Earlier in the month crowned the winner of the AL's 1981 Cy Young Award, Fingers saved 28 games while posting a microscopic 1.04 ERA. Photo: User laffy4k on Flickr (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 1975: The Minnesota Twins Hire Veteran Former National League Skipper Gene
item.description: The Minnesota Twins hire veteran former National League skipper Gene Mauch as their manager for 1976. He fills a vacancy created on September 29 when Frank Quilici was dismissed following 3½ years at the Twins' helm, a term which produced a mark since July 7, 1972. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1974: Rangers First Baseman Mike Hargrove, Who Hit .323 With 66 RBI
item.description: Rangers first baseman Mike Hargrove, who hit .323 with 66 RBI and a .395 OBP, is voted American League Rookie of the Year with 16 of 23 first place votes, with the others going to Bucky Dent (3), George Brett (2), Rick Burleson (1) and Jim Sundberg (1). Photo: Peter Roan (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 1972: Pittsburgh Pirates Right Fielder Roberto Clemente Wins His 12th
item.description: Pittsburgh Pirates right fielder Roberto Clemente wins his 12th consecutive Gold Glove Award and Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Wes Parker his sixth in a row. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1970: New York Yankees Catcher Thurman Munson Receives 23 of 24 First-Place
item.description: New York Yankees catcher Thurman Munson receives 23 of 24 first-place votes and is named American League Rookie of the Year. Munson batted .302 with six home runs and 53 RBI in 132 games during the regular season. Cleveland Indians outfielder Roy Foster (.268, 23, 60) is also named on a first place ballot. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1970: Gerald Nugent, 78, President and Majority Owner of the Philadelphia
item.description: Gerald Nugent, 78, president and majority owner of the Philadelphia Phillies from 1932 to 1942.

item.title: 1966: Cincinnati Reds Infielder Tommy Helms Is Voted National League Rookie
item.description: Cincinnati Reds infielder Tommy Helms is voted National League Rookie of the Year with 12 of 20 first place votes, with the others going to Sonny Jackson (3), Tito Fuentes (2), Randy Hundley (1), Larry Jaster (1) and Cleon Jones (1). Photo: Don Hunter (Public domain).

item.title: 1958: Chicago Cubs Slugger Ernie Banks, Who Batted .313
item.description: Chicago Cubs slugger Ernie Banks, who batted .313 with 47 home runs and 129 RBI, is named National League Most Valuable Player. Willie Mays of the San Francisco Giants is the runner-up, after going .347, 29, 96. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1949: Boston Red Sox Left Fielder Ted Williams
item.description: Boston Red Sox left fielder Ted Williams, who lost the Triple Crown when his batting average was .0002 below that of George Kell, wins the American League MVP Award with 13 of 22 first place votes, with the rest of the votes going to Phil Rizzuto (5), Joe Page (3) and Mel Parnell (1). Photo: Bowman Gum (Public domain).

item.title: 1948: Lou Boudreau, 31-Year-Old Shortstop
item.description: Lou Boudreau, 31-year-old shortstop and player-manager of the world champion Cleveland Indians, wins the 1948 American League Most Valuable Player Award; he earns 22 of 24 first-place votes and bests runner-up Joe DiMaggio by 81 points in BBWAA balloting. Boudreau batted .355 with 199 hits, 18 homers (including a pair in the AL's pennant-clinching tie-breaker game), and 106 runs batted in. Photo: RF (Public domain).

item.title: 1945: A Team of Negro Leagues All-Stars, Including Jackie Robinson
item.description: A team of Negro leagues all-stars, including Jackie Robinson and Roy Campanella, travel to Venezuela for the Serie Monumental, where they will play several Venezuelan all-star teams.

item.title: 1944: In 1944, the Award Was Named After Kenesaw Mountain Landis
item.description: In 1944, the award was named after Kenesaw Mountain Landis, the first Commissioner of Baseball, who served from 1920 until his death on November 25, 1944.

item.title: 1942: The Baltimore Sun Reports That a Group of Local Businessmen Has
item.description: The Baltimore Sun reports that a group of local businessmen has organized to buy the Philadelphia Phils from destitute owner Gerald Nugent and move them to the Maryland metropolis; the group plans to meet with mayor Howard W. Jackson in the coming days. The National League is brokering a sale of the struggling franchise, although league chief Ford Frick opposes its relocation.

item.title: 1940: The New York Giants Acquire Second Baseman Joe Orengo From the St
item.description: The New York Giants acquire second baseman Joe Orengo from the St. Louis Cardinals in a cash transaction. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1930: The Sporting News, Acting to Fill the Most Valuable Player Void
item.description: The Sporting News, acting to fill the Most Valuable Player void, announces its selection of Washington Senators shortstop Joe Cronin in the American League and New York Giants first baseman Bill Terry in the National League. Photo: Harris & Ewing (Public domain).

item.title: 1889: Former Indianapolis Hoosiers Shortstop Jack Glasscock
item.description: Former Indianapolis Hoosiers shortstop Jack Glasscock, claiming that his pledge to the Players' League does not constitute a binding contract, becomes the first defection from the Brotherhood when he signs with the New York Giants of the National League, thus becoming the first "double jumper" in major league history. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).
